chapter: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
title: Roy Eldridge sits in at Pittsburgh and Horace teaches him to read
summary: Roy Eldridge showed up in a ragged coat with a battered horn, blew on 'I Got Rhythm', and Horace taught him to read; he stayed in Horace's band for years and later followed him to Fletcher's Grand Terrace.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Well, he recently was in Denver here at the Warehouse with the great Ella Fitzgerald, and I think he came in as an extra added attraction because he plays solos (soul, whatnot, and -- but there's a guy, I feel like I've always been closer to him, more than quite a few musicians because I remember Roy when I first had my band in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Roy is from a little town out of Pittsburgh called Duquesne, which the great Earl Hines came from. And Roy came in one day to the Hotel where we were stopping called Patters Pontos Hotel on Wiley Avenue. I'll never forget it. And he came in and made himself known. We were rehearsing and everything.

And he says, 'Hey man, I'm a trumpet player, can I sit in?' you know, one of those kind of things. And I looked at him, man; he had his little raggedy coat on, all this kind of stuff. I said, 'look at this cat.' You should have seen the horn. The horn was really raggedy. The bell was about half as big as it should have been, and the middle valve was off. That's -- this is what intrigued me. The little cap on it, you know, the little screw, that was off.
And I looked at that horn and I said to myself, I
said, 'Now this guy's putting me on.' (Laughter)

He thinks he can play, you know. So I said, 'Okay,' I said, 'Well, we're going to play some things.' I said, 'What do you want to play?' He said, 'What do you want to play?' So this got me guy. He said, 'Let's play something up.' That meant fast, you know what I'm saying. I said, 'Well, how about a little I Got Rhythm?' He says, 'Solid, man.' He struck out on it, man, and this cat blew the bells off, and after that first, man, so I decided to slip a little music in front of him, you know, the section. It was Greek to him, you know. He could spell, you know, but I mean read -- so there was no problem there because I had some good guys who could read. And I thought I could -- as long as he knew his scale, you know, whole notes and whole notes, and he knew his positions, and that was easy.

So I took him under my wing and taught him to read, man, and the guy just blew. And we made trips one nighters, and he broke it up, and he was in my band for quite a few years. Then, of course, I would always tell my brother, you know, about anybody great like that. And when I rejoined my brother, I took Roy with me, and we got this Chicago job at the Grand Terrace -- Roy Eldridge and Chu Berry and joined John Fletcher, and, of course, there was quite a story behind that, you know. John Fletcher was broadcasting, and we had this

" Christopher Columbus " as the theme song. Roy was in that band, and he really played. And funny thing about it, just a few weeks ago we were right here in Denver reminiscing, all this, all of those old times, and, well, since Roy was with me, you know, he toured with Basie and went to Europe on his own with Lockjaw Davis, you know, about seven pieces, small group. They broke it up. And, of course, he's got places where he can play anytime, you know, and he's traveled extensively, and he's just matured quite a bit.
